oneSentence: A decoding setting that limits each next-token choice to the smallest group whose combined probability reaches a chosen threshold, such as 0.9.
plainExplanation:
When a language model generates text, it first assigns a probability to many possible next tokens. A token is a small unit of text, such as a word, part of a word, or punctuation. Top-p controls which of those candidate tokens are allowed to be sampled.

The model sorts candidate tokens from most likely to least likely, then keeps adding them until their probabilities add up to the chosen threshold p. If p is 0.9, it keeps the smallest set whose total probability is at least 0.9. The next token is then sampled only from that set, not from the full vocabulary.

This means the size of the allowed set changes from step to step. If probability is concentrated in a few tokens, only a few may be included. If probability is spread across many tokens, more may be included. That is the main difference from top-k, which always keeps a fixed number k of tokens.

What comes out is not a new score but a filtered token choice process. Lower top-p narrows the candidate set and can reduce variation, but it can also make output repetitive or narrow. Higher top-p includes more lower-probability options and can increase variety. Neither setting by itself guarantees safer or more accurate output. Top-p is often adjusted together with temperature, but they are different controls.

everydayAnalogy.title: Letting a playlist choose the next song
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine a music app ranks possible next songs by how well each fits the current playlist. With a 90% threshold, it keeps the smallest group whose probabilities add up to at least 90%, adjusts the probabilities within that group and makes a weighted random choice. If one or two songs are strong matches, the group is small. If many songs are similarly plausible, the group is larger.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: People in a meeting can explain their reasons and may look back at the full discussion. A language model does not do that in the same way here. It is applying probabilities token by token. Also, in real note-taking, whole phrases are chosen at once, while top-p usually operates on one token at a time, so the analogy hides the very small step size.

visual.title: How top-p keeps a changing set of next-token options
visual.learningObjective: Show why top-p does not keep a fixed number of tokens, but a fixed probability mass that can produce a small or large candidate set.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram. Start with ranked next-token candidates and their probabilities. Then accumulate probability from highest to lowest until the chosen threshold is reached. Highlight the kept nucleus set and grey out the rest. End by showing sampling from only the kept set. Include one case where the set is small and one where it is larger.

steps.label: Rank candidates
steps.explanation: List possible next tokens from most likely to least likely, each with a probability from the model.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a vertical list of 6 to 8 tokens with horizontal probability bars, sorted descending. Use clear labels such as token A 0.50, token B 0.25, token C 0.10, and so on.

steps.label: Accumulate probability
steps.explanation: Add probabilities from the top down until the running total reaches the chosen threshold p, such as 0.90.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a running-total column beside the bars. Animate or indicate cumulative sums: 0.50, 0.75, 0.85, 0.91. Draw a threshold line at p = 0.90.

steps.label: Form the nucleus
steps.explanation: Keep only the smallest set that reaches the threshold. Remove lower-probability tokens from consideration for this step.
steps.visualInstruction: Highlight the included rows up to the first row that crosses the threshold. Grey out all remaining rows and label them excluded this step.

steps.label: Sample within the nucleus
steps.explanation: Choose the next token only from the kept set, with more likely tokens still favoured inside that set.
steps.visualInstruction: Show arrows only from highlighted tokens to an output token slot. Use thicker arrows for higher probabilities. Keep excluded rows disconnected.

steps.label: Repeat with a new distribution
steps.explanation: At the next position in the text, probabilities change, so the nucleus may contain fewer or more tokens than before.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a second small panel with a flatter distribution where more rows are needed to reach p = 0.90. Add a note: top-p set size changes step by step.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal the running total and see which tokens enter the nucleus at different probability shapes; a toggle switches between a sharp distribution and a flat one.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains top-p in five steps. First, it shows possible next tokens ranked by probability. Second, it adds those probabilities from the top downward until the total reaches a threshold such as 0.90. Third, it keeps only the smallest group of tokens needed to reach that total and excludes the rest. Fourth, it shows that the model samples only from the kept group, still favouring higher-probability tokens. Fifth, it compares two cases: when the distribution is sharp, only a few tokens are kept; when it is flatter, more tokens are needed. The main point is that top-p keeps a changing number of tokens based on total probability, unlike top-k, which keeps a fixed count.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-panel diagram with highlighted cumulative totals and shaded excluded tokens. Two side examples show that a peaked distribution leads to a small nucleus, while a flatter distribution leads to a larger nucleus.

workedExample.scenario: The model is generating the next token after: "The revised talking points will be circulated by".
workedExample.input: Candidate tokens and probabilities are: " noon" 0.42, " email" 0.24, " close" 0.11, " 18" 0.08, " Monday" 0.06 and "." 0.03. All remaining tokens together account for 0.06. Use top-p = 0.80.
process: Sort the individual tokens from highest to lowest probability.
Add probabilities in order. The cumulative totals are 0.42, 0.66, 0.77 and then 0.85.
Stop at the smallest prefix that reaches at least 0.80. Retain " noon", " email", " close" and " 18".
Renormalise those four probabilities over their total of 0.85. Their sampling weights become about 49.4%, 28.2%, 12.9% and 9.4%.
Sample one token using those adjusted weights. At the following step, the model produces a new distribution and constructs a new nucleus.
workedExample.result: " noon" is the likeliest selection, but any of the four retained tokens can be sampled. The number of candidates at the next step may differ because top-p applies to the new probability distribution.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A desk officer in a small field presence with intermittent connectivity is using an approved, locally hosted model to tighten talking points before informals resume in 20 minutes.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The desk officer compares top-p settings to keep the drafting reasonably consistent without forcing identical wording each time. A lower value narrows the candidate set; a higher value may admit more varied phrasing. The setting affects variation, not whether the output is accurate or cleared.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Talking points may contain uncleared positions or attribution-sensitive details. Do not enter them into any tool not approved for that material. Even in an approved system, top-p is not a factuality or confidentiality control. The desk officer must check the draft against the cleared file.

whyItMatters: Top-p affects how risky, varied and review-heavy generated text may be. If you set it too low, outputs can become narrow, repetitive or brittle. If you set it too high, outputs may wander into weaker wording or unsupported details. For anyone choosing model settings, evaluating assistants or comparing vendors, top-p is one of the controls that changes behaviour without changing the underlying model weights. It is especially important in tasks where consistency matters, such as drafting summaries, and in tasks where some variation is useful, such as brainstorming alternative phrasing. Knowing top-p also helps you separate two questions that are often mixed together: how the model scores options, and how a system chooses among them.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Top-p and top-k are the same setting with different names.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related but not the same. Top-k keeps exactly k highest-probability tokens every time. Top-p keeps as many tokens as needed to reach a probability threshold, so the number kept changes from step to step. Some tools list both because they can be combined.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A top-p value of 0.9 means the chosen token has a 90 percent chance of being correct.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It does not measure correctness. It only defines the pool of allowed tokens by cumulative probability. The selected token can still be wrong, awkward or misleading, because the model may assign high probability to poor continuations in some contexts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Lowering top-p always improves factual accuracy.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Lower top-p usually reduces randomness, but it does not make the model reliable by itself. If the highest-probability continuation is inaccurate, a lower top-p can make that inaccurate continuation more likely to appear again. Accuracy depends on the model, the prompt, the context and any retrieval or verification steps.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Top-p changes what the model has learned.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Top-p does not retrain the model or alter its weights. It only changes the decoding stage, which is the procedure used to pick the next token from the probabilities the model already produced.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Top-p tells the system to choose the next piece of text only from the most likely options whose probabilities add up to a chosen amount, such as 90 percent.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: At each decoding step, the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token. Under nucleus sampling, tokens are sorted by probability in descending order, and the smallest prefix whose cumulative probability is at least p is retained. The distribution is then renormalised over that retained set, and one token is sampled from it. Because the retained prefix depends on the shape of the distribution, the effective candidate count varies by step. In a peaked distribution, the nucleus may contain only a few tokens; in a flatter distribution, it may contain many. This distinguishes top-p from top-k, which clips by rank rather than cumulative mass. In practice, top-p also interacts with temperature, because temperature reshapes the distribution before or during sampling, which changes how many tokens are needed to reach the threshold.

keyTakeaway: Top-p retains the smallest set of likely next tokens whose combined probability reaches the threshold, then samples from that set. Its size can change at every step.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best distinguishes top-p from top-k during text generation?
options: Top-p keeps a fixed number of highest-probability tokens, while top-k keeps a fixed probability mass.
Top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities reach a threshold, while top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens.
Top-p changes the model weights during generation, while top-k changes only the prompt.
Top-p guarantees fewer hallucinations than top-k because it removes all unlikely tokens.
quickCheck.explanation: Top-p clips by cumulative probability, so the kept set can grow or shrink depending on the distribution. Top-k clips by rank, so it always keeps exactly k tokens. Neither setting retrains the model, and neither guarantees factual accuracy.

issues.problem: The page equates a concentrated next-token distribution with the model being "very confident" and a flatter distribution with it being "uncertain." Probability concentration is not a calibrated measure of confidence or correctness. A peaked distribution can still strongly favour a wrong continuation.
issues.fix: Replace the confidence language with a description of distribution shape: "If probability is concentrated in a few tokens, only a few may be included. If probability is spread across many tokens, more may be included."

issues.problem: The claim that lower top-p "usually makes output safer" is unsupported and conflicts with the later explanation that lowering top-p does not reliably improve accuracy. Top-p narrows the sampling pool, but safety and factual accuracy do not change monotonically with it.
issues.fix: Replace the final paragraph with: "What comes out is not a new score but a filtered token choice process. Lower top-p narrows the candidate set and can reduce variation, but it can also make output repetitive or narrow. Higher top-p includes more lower-probability options and can increase variety. Neither setting by itself guarantees safer or more accurate output. Top-p is often adjusted together with temperature, but they are different controls."

issues.problem: The objective says top-p keeps a "fixed probability mass." It actually uses a fixed threshold. The retained mass can exceed p because the final included token may take the cumulative total past the threshold. The worked example retains 0.85 when p is 0.80.
issues.fix: Show why top-p does not keep a fixed number of tokens, but uses a fixed probability threshold that can produce a small or large candidate set.

issues.problem: The wording frames top-p as a direct control over risk and unsupported details. Top-p can affect which continuations are available, but it does not provide a reliable safety or factuality control.
issues.fix: State that top-p changes variation and review needs, while neither low nor high values guarantee factual or safe output.

issues.problem: The phrase "changes with the model’s confidence" repeats the false identification of distribution shape with calibrated confidence.
issues.fix: Top-p controls variety by keeping enough likely tokens to reach a probability threshold, so the number of options changes with the probability distribution.
